subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Sunk Cost Fallacy
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Sunk Cost Fallacy.

hook.text: You've watched two hours of a terrible movie. You stay because you've already invested the time. Why?

buildup.text: The sunk cost fallacy: continuing a course of action because of past investment, not future value.

discovery.text: Rational thinking says only future costs and benefits matter. Past spending is gone and can't be recovered.

twist.text: Companies throw billions into failing projects because admitting the loss feels worse than losing more.

climax.text: The Concorde jet continued despite guaranteed losses. "We've come too far to stop" is always a red flag.

punchline.text: What's spent is spent. Decide from now, not from then.

quiz.question: What is the sunk cost fallacy?
options: Continuing because of past investment rather than future value

details.summary: The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to continue investing in a failing course of action because of what has already been spent rather than future returns.
details.whyItMatters: The sunk cost fallacy traps people in bad relationships, failing projects, and losing investments. Recognizing it enables better decisions by focusing on what lies ahead rather than what is already lost.
takeaways: Past investments irrationally influence future decisions
Rational choices should consider only future costs and benefits
Emotional attachment to prior effort drives the fallacy

faq.question: Why is it so hard to abandon a sunk cost?
faq.answer: Abandoning a sunk cost feels like admitting failure and wasting prior effort. Loss aversion makes the psychological pain of writing off an investment feel worse than continuing to pour resources in. Social pressure and public commitment amplify the effect.

faq.question: What is a real-world example of the sunk cost fallacy?
faq.answer: The Concorde jet continued receiving massive funding despite clear evidence it would never be profitable, simply because so much had already been invested. This is why the sunk cost fallacy is sometimes called the Concorde fallacy. Similar patterns appear in wars, startups, and personal projects.
